basis: Ushojo muure died matches the independent Shinaic mur/muṛ perfective and mr̥tá rather than the present mar stem; finite ending e is retained as a cell distinction.
Ushojo khaa eat and khe bites preserve the kh root and semantic range of khā́dati; the imperative/present cells are separate from inherited finite accent.
Ushojo suto slept agrees segmentally and grammatically with suptá perfective, including pt simplification and final agreement vowel. Raw English/form boundary corrected separately.
Ushojo pii drank is securely the drink root shared with píbati-family forms, but the past cell is not a direct reflex of the reduplicated present headword.

Brokskat bazun matches Shina bazon spring in segmental structure and one of the source's explicitly co-listed senses; afternoon/summer are source polysemy and are retained, not separate cognate observations.
Ushojo buto all exactly matches the Shina buto quantifier family; bahutva9190 remains an independent alternative, so the precise old formation is not selected by accent.

Brokskat pinili and Ushojo piwal ant share the pi...l insect stem with Shina pibilli/philili and pipīlá derivatives. Brokskat medial n requires dissimilation or a derivative variant; retain that segmental uncertainty.
Ushojo ṭhoŋgo axe is closely matched by Palula ṭhoṅgi axe and the ṭaṅka implement family; final o/i reflects a formation or gender difference, not identity of cells.
Ushojo kacato bad matches Shina kʌc̣aṭo bad in the kicca dirt/dirty family. It is a derived adjective with a further t/o formation, not a simple mud noun.

Ushojo kela banana matches the regional kadala/kela banana family. The survey initial stress differs from Kundal final kelá, but regional borrowing must be tested before treating this as inherited accent divergence.
Ushojo ḍɛṛ belly closely matches Shina ḍeer and the independently reconstructed ḍhiḍḍha belly family, including retroflexes and medial-cluster reduction.

Brokskat wor belly plausibly continues udára via the independently attested Shina uar/ūar type and consonant loss, with rounding or glide formation. This is a proposed link, not an author-supplied etymology.
Ushojo baṛo big matches Shina baṛo and vaḍra/vaḍḍa-type big adjectives; the final o and initial stress are observed independently of the unaccented old reconstruction.

Brokskat zozi/zuruzii birch are compared with Shina juẓ/joẓi and bhūrja derivatives. Initial bh loss and the zuru- variant require dialectal history; treat the family link as provisional, not a strict old-accent training item.

Primary SchmidtKaul2008p275Table2item201 really prints Brokskat c̣ito beside tiito. c̣ito matches the inherited Shina tiktá family; both are first-syllable stressed, but no Brokskat mora reading is claimed.

SchmidtKaul2008p247 explicitly identifies Brokskat tiito bitter as a Kashmiri loan; p275 confirms the form. Its ultimate tiktá family is retained for lexical comparison, with borrowing excluded from direct inherited accent tests.

Brokskat kyono and Ushojo kinono black match the Shina kino family from kr̥ṣṇá. Ushojo has an additional no syllable requiring derivative or repetitive morphology; do not collapse the syllable counts.

Brokskat lyl and Ushojo ɫuɫ blood match Shina leel blood assigned by Schmidt to lōhila11168. The related lṓhita11165 is an alternative formation; do not choose its known accent solely to fit a monosyllable.

Brokskat aati and Ushojo ʌnṭhi bone agree with Shina nasalized aṭi and the aṣṭhi/ásthi bone family, preserving the final i and characteristic dental/retroflex cluster outcome. The old accent and nasal variant require formation-level treatment.
Ushojo pho boy directly matches Palula pho/phoo boy in the pōta family. The old pṓta/pōtaka variants and singular/plural history are retained, and the unmarked monosyllable supplies no mora accent.
